name: Liberal socialism
summary: Liberal socialism holds that liberalism and socialism, properly understood, are not opposed: socialism is liberty extended to the poor, and liberty without a minimum of economic security is empty. It seeks equal political and civil rights together with a fairer distribution of wealth, workers' share in running production and income tied to work rather than ownership. It reaches these by the democratic method of majority rule, respect for the opposition and gradual reform, in a mixed economy of public, municipal, cooperative and private enterprise, and rejects both laissez-faire capitalism and centralised, dictatorial socialism.
scope: The tradition the defining sources name: Carlo Rosselli's Socialismo liberale (1930) and Guido Calogero's liberalsocialismo (Manifesto del liberalsocialismo, 1940), which Michele Donno's entry in the Dizionario del liberalismo italiano treats as the two Italian strands of the name, and John Stuart Mill's late socialism, which Matthew McManus's account presents as the tradition's mature 19th-century form. Mill's texts are used only where they set out his socialist views (Principles of Political Economy IV.7, the posthumous Chapters on Socialism, the Autobiography's account of his socialism); his wider liberal writings are not used. Social liberalism (Hobhouse), Keynes, Rawls, the Action Party and Giustizia e Libertà's programmes, ethical socialism and the parties sometimes called liberal socialist are not used: the defining sources name them as related or as later uses, not as the ideology's own texts.

name: Socialismo liberale
aliases.quote: Per «socialismo liberale» si intende quel filone di socialismo non marxista che tende a dissociare il socialismo dal marxismo

name: Liberalsocialismo
aliases.quote: Il «liberalsocialismo» è, invece, più che una conciliazione del liberalismo con il socialismo, il superamento dialettico del socialismo e del liberalismo in una sintesi nuova

keyFigures.role: Author of Socialismo liberale (1930) and founder of Giustizia e Libertà.
keyFigures.quote: Nel suo saggio Socialismo liberale , Rosselli si domanda cosa sia il liberalismo

keyFigures.role: Founder of the 1936 Movimento liberalsocialista and author of Ricordi del liberalsocialismo.
keyFigures.quote: Guido Calogero nei suoi Ricordi del liberalsocialismo (1944) indica tale data nel 1936, con la nascita del Movimento liberalsocialista

keyFigures.role: Liberal philosopher who called himself a socialist; McManus calls him the tradition's most articulate spokesman.
keyFigures.quote: reached its maturity in the 19th century with John Stuart Mill, its most articulate and well-known spokesman

sources.usedFor: Mill's account of his socialism (chapter VII): work for all, common ownership of the raw material of the globe.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Calogero's manifesto rejects distinctions of caste in rights and laws and fights the idle enjoyment of inherited wealth.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Mill expected the wage relation to be superseded by workers' associations, but Rosselli keeps capitalist, individual and family enterprise alongside cooperatives.

alienated-labor.rationale: Rosselli says rationalised, mechanised production sacrifices the worker's personality and that wage earners lack any dignity or responsibility at work.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Calogero makes an 'armed liberalism' against fascism the universal basis of political life, and Rosselli frames the fight against fascism as the struggle for liberty itself.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Calogero says liberty is only for those who work for it and its enemies meet force and coercion, while Rosselli asks socialists to respect the right of opposition on any ground.

ban-interest.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants no legitimacy recognised for the private possession and use of the pure interest on capital.

bound-labor.rationale: Mill rejects the theory of dependence and protection, in which the poor are guided by their superiors, in favour of the labourers' self-dependence.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Rosselli says reality disproved Marx's expected catastrophic crisis and accepts Sombart's forecast that capitalism will keep dominating important branches for a long time.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Rosselli credits the bourgeoisie with having once carried liberty and progress, breaking the closed feudal world against Church and king.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants everyone to share equally in the freedom to express their personality in every conceivable form, with freedom of thought and press.

central-planning.rationale: Rosselli says the Russian experience ended the old centralising collectivist programme, Calogero calls total collectivism economically unworkable, and Mill calls running a whole country's industry from a single centre chimerical.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Rosselli calls liberalism historicist, seeing nothing as fixed and condemning attempts to freeze the social order.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants aid for the weak and sick paid from wealth held by society in state, provincial, municipal and cooperative forms.

class-collaboration.rationale: Rosselli says socialists in government must soften their class concept and govern for all, with a role for progressive sections of the bourgeoisie, yet he also wants liberalism to take up the proletarian struggle.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Rosselli rejects Marx's materialist account of history and says fascism cannot be explained by class interest alone; Calogero wants socialism freed from the myth of historical materialism.

clerical-rule.rationale: Calogero's manifesto derives every legal norm from the citizens' will and wants equal rights regardless of religion.

collective-farming.rationale: Rosselli faults Marxists for ignoring Italy's small owners, tenants and sharecroppers and condemns Soviet agrarian policy for squeezing the peasant.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Calogero's manifesto rejects imperialism and calls for the economic internationalisation of the colonies and of the great sources of raw materials.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Rosselli says the only source of legitimate power lies in the whole people, and Calogero derives every legal norm from the citizens' will.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Calogero wants people to curb the taste for possessing beyond the common average, and McManus contrasts liberal socialism's developmental ethic with the view that the good life comes from production and consumption.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Mill says communism and similar community schemes must first prove themselves by experiment, and Rosselli and Calogero keep national, municipal and private forms alongside cooperatives.

corporate-influence.rationale: McManus says liberal socialists deny property rights that enable political plutocracy and push back on plutocratic rule.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants society's common wealth to give special help to everyone in a position of inferiority, and McManus lists a generous welfare state among liberal socialism's forms.

democracy-best.rationale: Rosselli says no reform is too bold if a majority accepts it and that the democratic method must be kept even under a stable socialist majority; Calogero derives every legal norm from the citizens' will by majority rule.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Rosselli calls struggle the very essence of life and political conflicts desirable when kept within the rules of the democratic method, with the right of opposition.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Rosselli says socialism without democracy means dictatorship and denies socialism's first aims; Calogero rejects the socialism that sees the dictatorship of the proletariat as the condition of future liberty.

direct-action.rationale: Rosselli makes acceptance of the liberal method of political struggle (universal suffrage, parliaments, peaceful conquest of power) the one fixed point of the socialist movement.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Rosselli places the only source of legitimate power in the people, and Calogero derives every norm from the citizens' will.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Rosselli makes recognition of an inviolable sphere of autonomy in each citizen a condition of the liberal method.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Calogero's founding principle assigns every other person a right equal to one's own, and his manifesto wants rights and laws equal without distinctions of religion, race, caste or wealth.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Calogero wants pay narrowed as solidarity grows and wealth shared equitably, while making pay proportional to work a first stage; McManus, quoting Walzer, says liberal socialists are serious about equality but not 'egalitarianist'.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Calogero makes liberty the universal basis of all political life, but Rosselli says the democratic method presupposes a high degree of civilisation that Italians still had to acquire.

experts-over-public.rationale: Rosselli holds that the free persuasion of the majority is the best way to reach truth, and that socialism must come from persuasion, not from the imposition of an enlightened minority.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Rosselli wants forms of enterprise fitted to each sector's traditions and technique, with no rigid programme, and Mill holds that socialist arrangements can only be tested by practical trial.

gradual-change.rationale: Rosselli wants socialisation reached gradually, by mediated steps, and Mill wants changes tried first on a small experimental scale.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants each person paid in proportion to their actual work, recognising the entrepreneur's real labour but not the private enjoyment of pure interest on capital.

independent-unions.rationale: Rosselli says subordinating the unions to the party harmed the parties, and that workers' democracy lives in the unions, not the party.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Rosselli praises the labour movement for demanding better machinery and methods, tying workers' advancement to higher social productivity.

informal-organisation.rationale: Rosselli wants the socialist movement organised as a broad federation of unions, cooperatives, mutual societies and cultural associations around a constructive programme.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants laws with no distinctions depending on religion.

job-guarantee.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants society's common wealth to guarantee everyone the right to take part in common work.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: Calogero denies legitimacy to income from the pure interest of capital while rewarding real work, and Mill expects labourers collectively owning the capital to replace the capitalist as chief.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Calogero's manifesto derives every legal norm from the will of the citizens expressed by majority rule.

leader-cult.rationale: Rosselli mocks Mussolini's boast of unanimity and calls fascism the autobiography of a nation that worships unanimity and longs for a providential leader.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Rosselli keeps public enterprise for essential public services and lists municipal forms, and McManus reports Mill backing municipal gas and water.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Rosselli and Calogero reject communist dictatorship and the leading role of a single party.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Calogero's manifesto keeps free competition wherever it works and restricts it wherever it does not, rejecting both absolute collectivism and absolute individualism; Rosselli likewise wants a mix of private, cooperative and public forms.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Rosselli's book is a sustained rejection of Marx's materialist determinism in favour of human will, and Calogero wants socialism freed from the myth of historical materialism.

means-match-ends.rationale: Rosselli calls liberty both the end and the means of socialism and sees a perfect harmony between ends and means; Calogero's second principle is to build socialism through liberty.

minority-veto.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants every legal norm to follow the citizens' will by majority rule, and Rosselli lets the majority change the social order so long as it respects the opposition.

moral-incentives.rationale: Calogero wants pay proportional to work so as not to dry up the taste for industry, while hoping that solidarity will let the gaps between pay narrow; Rosselli calls socialism first of all a moral revolution.

municipal-property.rationale: Rosselli and Calogero want a mix of state, municipal, cooperative and private forms rather than exclusive local ownership.

nation-first.rationale: Calogero's manifesto rejects nationalism and holds nations to the same duties of honesty and respect for others' rights as individuals.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Calogero's manifesto rejects both absolute collectivism and absolute individualism, and Rosselli rejects both bourgeois liberalism and communist dictatorship.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Rosselli calls force used to defend the democratic order against reactionary attack fully legitimate.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Rosselli condemns bourgeois liberalism's dogma of the state as an organ of police and defence, and Calogero's manifesto wants the law to regulate wages, hours and companies.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rosselli requires socialists in power to respect dissenting minorities and the right of opposition, and Calogero's manifesto lists freedom of party as a foundation of self-government.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Rosselli calls the fight against fascism a revolutionary struggle, Calogero makes 'armed liberalism' part of the programme, and Donno notes the right of resistance against violence used on the majority.

organic-representation.rationale: Rosselli's liberal method rests on the representative system and the alternation of parties in power, and Calogero lists freedom of party among the foundations of self-government.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Rosselli says the people's will, the only source of legitimate power, is expressed in parliaments elected by universal suffrage.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: Rosselli says the democratic method, with power won by majority through universal suffrage, will sooner or later bring socialists to power, and Donno stresses his rejection of insurrection.

participatory-democracy.rationale: McManus names highly participatory institutions reaching into the economy as a core liberal socialist commitment, and Rosselli asks for workers' share in running production.

party-controls-media.rationale: Calogero's manifesto requires freedom of thought and of the press as the basis of mutual control and self-government, and Rosselli lists press freedom among the rights the liberal method protects.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Rosselli says discipline belongs to action, though it must never be imposed in the realm of ideas.

party-own-road.rationale: Rosselli says each country's socialist movement takes its own national form and that Italian socialism must free itself from imported Marxist schemes to fit Italian conditions.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Rosselli says Italian socialism must break the nationalist parties' monopoly on patriotism and that denying the homeland is an error that hands it to the right.

pay-for-effort.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants pay matched to each person's actual work and toil.

person-over-state.rationale: Rosselli condemns a state raised to an end with man degraded to a mere means and requires sacred respect for the person.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: Calogero's manifesto derives legal norms from the citizens' will by majority rule.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Rosselli expects a federation of nations to grow from the national communities, and Calogero wants citizenship rights extended beyond single nations and colonies internationalised economically.

positive-liberty.rationale: Rosselli writes that liberty without a minimum of economic autonomy is a mere phantom, and Calogero's manifesto refuses to pair freedom of speech and vote with the freedom to starve.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Rosselli calls the homeland the expression of a shared history and destiny and wants socialists to take up the higher values of national life instead of leaving them to nationalist parties.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Rosselli says formal political liberties have little value for those kept in misery, and Calogero calls it hypocrisy to offer those fighting poverty only the freedom to opine and vote.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Rosselli calls the liberal socialist a socialist above all by active commitment to the cause of the poor and oppressed, and Calogero wants special help for all who are in a position of inferiority.

production-for-use.rationale: Rosselli says socialists ask, in the name of liberty, for the criterion of collective utility to replace that of private gain, and expects regulated economies in which meeting needs prevails over profit to spread.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Calogero denies legitimacy to income from the pure interest of capital, but Rosselli rejects Marx's economics and keeps the entrepreneur's reward for real work.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Calogero's manifesto commits liberal socialism to defending every body that can help realise liberty and justice in the world.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants equal and stable laws and a certain, impartial and independent administration of justice.

property-franchise.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants rights and laws equal with no distinction by wealth (censo) and an equal right for all to vote.

property-fundamental.rationale: Calogero denies any legitimacy to private income from the pure interest of capital, Mill holds that the idea of property is variable and may be reformed for the general good, and McManus says liberal socialists give productive property far less weight than classical liberals.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Mill writes that the laws of property must rest on their conduciveness to the general welfare, and Calogero ties ownership of the means of production to the reward of real work.

public-ownership.rationale: Rosselli says socialists now think poorly of the state as industrialist except for essential public services, and McManus reports Mill backing state railways and municipal gas and water.

racial-franchise.rationale: Calogero's manifesto gives every person an equal right to vote and wants rights free of distinctions by race.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants equal and stable rights and laws with no distinctions by religion, race, caste or wealth.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Rosselli calls the liberal socialist a believer, socialist above all by faith and sentiment, and says religions and metaphysics will never be abolished.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants laws governing the administration of joint-stock companies and workers' hours and wages, taken out of the private discretion of directors and employers.

religion-illusion.rationale: Rosselli calls it ridiculous to expect people ever to abolish religions and metaphysics and denies any necessary link between socialism and materialism.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Rosselli says that when one side breaks the democratic pact, force used by the majority is legitimate, a duty according to liberal doctrine from Blackstone to Mill; Donno stresses that he kept the right of resistance.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Mill set as the social problem of the future to unite individual liberty with common ownership of the raw material of the globe.

restore-past-order.rationale: Rosselli calls liberalism historicist, seeing history as perpetual becoming, and condemns the bourgeois attempt to halt it at the present stage.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Calogero's manifesto says that to offer people under dictatorship a higher standard of living without liberty is perfidy.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Rosselli asks socialism for a bath of realism, with no rigid programmes and constant revision in the light of experience; Mill holds that only practical trial can test socialist arrangements.

say-in-proportion-to-effect.rationale: McManus says that, for liberal socialists, what affects all should in part be decided by all.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Calogero's manifesto asks people to suppress the taste for gaining and possessing far beyond the common average and to cultivate the taste for working and producing.

separated-powers.rationale: McManus counts checks and balances on state power among liberal socialism's commitments, and Calogero wants an independent, impartial administration of justice.

single-common-good.rationale: Rosselli sees history as a perpetual clash of forces and calls political struggles inevitable and even desirable, to be kept within the rules of the democratic method.

social-market-economy.rationale: Calogero keeps free competition where it works and regulates it elsewhere, with social wealth used for the weak; Rosselli rejects both laissez-faire and the state as universal manager.

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: Rosselli writes that the spectre of violent social revolution now frightens only sparrows and shopkeepers and helps reaction.

socialized-markets.rationale: Mill wants markets with worker-owned associations, but Rosselli and Calogero also keep private, individual and capitalist firms wherever competition works.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Calogero's manifesto wants equal and stable laws, a certain and impartial judiciary and every norm derived from the citizens' will.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Rosselli says emancipation must be of body and soul together and that socialism must reaffirm the eternal values of the spirit.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Rosselli says the bourgeoisie now accepts the people as the only source of legitimate power and that parties in power must govern for all, not for one class.

state-harmful.rationale: Rosselli ends liberty in a state of free and equal citizens, and Calogero wants social wealth held in state, provincial, municipal and cooperative forms, so the state is kept, not abolished.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Rosselli rejects any official philosophy of socialism and attacks the old Marxist insistence on atheist positivism.

strong-leader.rationale: Rosselli treats the call for a duce or providential ruler as the servility that produced fascism and defines the liberal method as self-government; Calogero blames liberals who longed for a strong state for letting dictatorship grow.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Rosselli asks socialists to respect dissenting minorities and the right of opposition even when they govern with a stable majority.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Calogero's manifesto says: no nationalism, no racism, no imperialism.

total-state.rationale: Rosselli condemns the fascist state raised to an end with man degraded to a means and rejects any official philosophy; Calogero's manifesto defends freedom of thought, press and association.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Calogero's manifesto calls for equal and stable rights and laws with no distinction by religion.

unions-good.rationale: Rosselli writes that workers' democracy lives in the trade unions and wants the new socialist movement built around the labour movement, unions and cooperatives.

universal-morality.rationale: Calogero's manifesto grounds liberal socialism in one ethical principle, the universal canon of every history and civilisation: recognising every other person's right as equal to one's own.

vanguard-party.rationale: Rosselli wants socialism built from below by persuasion, never imposed by an enlightened minority, and calls a party that imposes distant ends a tendency toward dictatorship.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Rosselli prefers a modest liberty for all to boundless liberty for the few at the many's expense, and McManus says liberal socialists deny property rights that lead to political plutocracy.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Rosselli makes action the liberal socialist's true motto and calls the struggle for liberty worth every sacrifice.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Mill looked forward to the rule that those who do not work shall not eat being applied impartially to all, not to paupers only.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: Rosselli wants the socialist party extended to the whole working population, peasants, tenants and small owners included, not only industrial workers.

worker-ownership.rationale: Mill expected the association of labourers collectively owning their capital to predominate in the end, and Calogero wants the pure owner to recede as workers become able to act as entrepreneurs.

workers-councils.rationale: Rosselli places the only source of legitimate power in the whole people, expressing its will in parliaments elected by universal suffrage.

workers-nation.rationale: Rosselli calls an internationalism that denies the homeland a mistake and says world solidarity can only come through national movements joined later in a federation of nations.

workers-own-party.rationale: Rosselli wants a socialist party modelled on the British Labour Party, built around the workers' movement.

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: Rosselli wants the socialist party to focus on immediate goals attainable within a few years under a constructive programme.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Rosselli backs workers' control, a share in running production and the democratisation of the factory, and McManus says liberal socialists extend democratic principles into the economy.

missingStatements.text: Parliamentary democracy and civil liberties are the necessary method for reaching socialism, not obstacles to it.
missingStatements.rationale: Rosselli's formula that liberalism is the method and socialism the aim, and his rejection of one-party dictatorship, make this the core claim.

missingStatements.text: Workers' associations should gradually replace the wage relationship between employer and employee.
missingStatements.rationale: Mill expected wage labour to give way to partnership and cooperative associations, arguing the evil lies in the subjection of labour to capital.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09), bringing a pre-rules audit up to rules 5. The first pass rested mostly on Wikipedia; this pass replaced it with the defining texts: Rosselli's Socialismo liberale (Italian full text), Calogero's 1940 Manifesto del liberalsocialismo, Mill's Principles IV.7, Chapters on Socialism and Autobiography, McManus's Aeon essay and Donno's dictionary entry. Earlier answers that rested on Wikipedia or on a general value and are not settled by these texts were nulled (reviewHistory keeps them). Themes searched: economy (ownership, competition, pay, inheritance, welfare, unions), government (majority rule, parliament, opposition, legitimacy), means (violence, revolution, gradualism), world (nation, internationalism, colonies, federation), society and culture (religion, class, materialism), and, without result, ecology, technology, gender, crime, immigration and foreign policy, on which the defining texts are silent. Not reached: Girometti's article on Bobbio's liberal socialism (flore.unifi.it) and Calabrò's article on Rosselli (media.fupress.com) both returned a bot check; Calogero's later Difesa del liberalsocialismo, Bobbio's essays and McManus's book are not open access. The Stanford entry on socialism was read but never names liberal socialism, so it is not cited. The Italian strands differ: Calogero's 'armed liberalism' denies liberty to its enemies while Rosselli asks socialists to respect any opposition, and Mill's hope that workers' associations will supersede wage labour goes further than Rosselli's mixed economy; those answers are 0 at low confidence.
